characterizations.result_summary: Fabricated polyimide aerogels presented onset of decomposition ranging from 422 to 621 °C.

evidence.source_sentence: Due to the sensitive relations between aerogel physical, thermal, and mechanical properties, improving the polyimide aerogels performance requires understanding of their structure to properties relations, along with introducing a robust method to tailor aerogels properties to achieve the optimum performance.
Based on the results, combination of rigid and flexible diamine monomers at varying fractions successfully tailored the properties of the hybrid diamine polyimide aerogels.
Keywords: Polyimide; Hybrid Aerogel; BPDA; PMDA; Mesoporous Solids;
However, the ODA-BPDA aerogels presented significantly lower shrinkage than PPDA-BPDAs.

Based on this, the higher shrinkage of BPDA backbone aerogels with increasing PPDA content is believed to be due to the greater chain rigidity, high planarity, and shorter chain length between cross-links of the PPDA-BPDA oligomers.<sup>13</sup> Such chain geometry allows the polymer chains to densely pack together.

Furthermore, the decreasing shrinkage of BPDA backbone aerogels with increasing ODA content is believed to be due to non-co-planarity of the ODA-BPDA oligomers due to existence of the oxygen linking groups between the phenyl rings.<sup>35,36</sup> The reduced shrinkage of PMDA backbone aerogels with increasing PPDA content is believed to be due to highly rigid nature of PPDA-PMDA bonding.<sup>20</sup>
However, due to the shorter chain length between the cross-links as well as the planarity of ODA-PMDA chains, addition of more flexible ODA monomers resulted in increased shrinkage.
Expressively, the BPDA backbone hybrid diamine aerogel with 25% ODA fraction (S7) presented even higher shrinkage than the PPDA-BPDA samples.

This suggests that at low ODA-BPDA content, rather than non-co-planarity and shorter crosslinks, the more flexible nature of ODA-BPDA chains plays the dominant role and as a result, increases the shrinkage.
As observed from Figure 3, except the PPDA-PMDA aerogels, the main shrinkage of the samples is occurred through the CO2 supercritical drying stage.
Among the studied aerogels, PPDA-PMDA presented the lowest shrinkage of 7.3%, which is believed to be due to highly rigid and brittle nature of PPDA-PMDA bonding.<sup>20</sup>
Among the studied aerogels, single diamine PPDA-PMDA and ODA-BPDA presented the lowest densities of 0.056 g/cm and 0.083 $\mathrm { g } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$, correspondingly.
Similar to shrinkage results, it was observed that addition of 25% fraction of the diverse diamine monomer to dense PPDA-BPDA and ODA-PMDA aerogels did not affect the aerogels density considerably.
Roughly, similar morphology of the S3 and S5 as well as S6 and S7 aerogels is also in agreement with this observation.

Therefore, the low density PPDA-PMDA and ODA-BPDA aerogels presented the highest open cell contents of 96.6% and 94.8% among the samples.
Furthermore, the S2 hybrid aerogels with 50% ODA fraction presented high open cell content of 94.6%.

By comparing the results of S2 hybrid aerogels with PPDA-PMDA (S1) aerogel, it can be observed that more than 82% increased density of the S2 aerogels resulted in only 2% decrease in open cell content.

Therefore, achieving polyimide aerogels with desired network structure requires accurate control of all sensitive processing variables at optimum level.
From Figure 5A to Figure 5J, it is observed that the PMDA backbone aerogels fiber thickness, chain length between the crosslinks, and the average pore size were decreased with increasing ODA content.
Among the PMDA backbone aerogels, the S1 and S2 aerogels with PPDA content of more than 50% presented roughly similar morphology as well as fiber thickness of about 45 nm.
However, increasing the ODA content from 75% in sample S3 to 87.5% in sample S4 resulted in major pore size reduction, as presented in Figure 5F and Figure 5H.

As observed from Figure 5K to Figure 5T, the average pore size and particle diameter of the BPDA backbone aerogels were increased with increasing ODA content.<sup>13,17</sup> Furthermore, the increased pore size with increasing ODA fraction of BPDA backbone aerogels was commensurate with shrinkage and open cell content trends of those samples.
Unlike ODA-BPDA (S10) sample with the fibrous structure, the hybrid BPDA backbone aerogels, samples S7 to S9, presented clusters of particles morphology closer to PPDA-BPDA (S6) sample.

The characteristic bands of polyimides, including 727 ( cm-1), $1 3 7 0 ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$(imide C−N), 1715 $( \mathsf { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$(symmetric imide C=O) and $1 7 7 5 ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$(asymmetric imide C=O) are observed for all studied samples.<sup>30</sup> None of the sample sets presented significant band of $1 8 6 0 ~ ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$, which indicates the existence of unreacted anhydride.

However, PMDA backbone aerogels presented small peaks at 1660 $\textstyle { \left( \cos ^ { - 1 } \right) }$(amic acid C=O) and $1 5 3 5 \ : \mathrm { ~ ( ~ c m } ^ { - 1 } )$(amide C−N) bands, which may suggest incomplete imidization of polyimide samples.

The lack of $1 6 6 0 \ ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$and $1 5 3 5 \ ( { \mathrm { c m } } ^ { - 1 } )$bands on BPDA backbone aerogels may indicate the complete imidization of those sample.
On both PMDA and BPDA aerogels, the hybrid samples somehow presented a combination of single diamine aerogel peaks with different intensities.
For instance, comparing the sample S7 with S6 presented that addition of ODA to PPDA-BPDA aerogels resulted in appearance of the peak at $1 2 3 8 ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$band.
Furthermore, for S7 to S10 aerogels, the intensity of the peak at $1 2 3 8 \ ( \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 1 } )$band increased with increasing ODA fraction.
As illustrated in Figure 8, fabricated polyimide aerogels presented high onset of decomposition ranging from 422 to $6 2 1 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$.
On PMDA backbone, the PPDA-PMDA (S1) and ODA-PMDA (S5) aerogels presented the lowest and highest onset of decomposition, respectively.
The decomposition trends of the PMDA backbone hybrid aerogels were also reminiscent the combination of single diamine S1 and S5 trends.
The PPDA-BPDA (S6) and ODA-BPDA (S10) presented the onset of decomposition of $6 2 1 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$and $5 8 9 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$, respectively.

The BPDA backbone hybrid aerogels presented the onset of decomposition ranging from 580 to $5 8 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$, those were close to the onset of decomposition of ODA-BPDA (S10) aerogels.

In general, at comparable backbone chemistry, polyimides containing highly reactive PPDA diamine were expected to present higher decomposition temperature than those containing ODA diamine monomer.<sup>13</sup> Similar tendency were observed from BPDA backbone aerogels in this work.

However, on PMDA backbone, the PPDA-PMDA (S1) aerogel presented lower onset of decomposition of $4 2 2 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$than the ODA-PMDA sample with decomposition temperature of $5 8 6 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$By a closer look to the decomposition trend of the PPDA-PMDA (S1) aerogels, two varying slopes of decomposition at less than $7 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$were observed.

Based on previous studies, the onset of decomposition of $6 3 2 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$was reported from nonporous PPDA-PMDA polyimide films, made at higher number of repeat units of $\mathrm { n } { > } 3 0 .
^ { 2 0 }$However, to achieve solid stable PPDA-PMDA sol-gels, the sample S1 was made from very low number of repeat unit of $\mathrm { n } { = } 1$in this work.

As altering number of repeat units has very minor effect on decomposition behavior of polyimides and the onset of decomposition would mainly affected by changes in the backbone chemistry,<sup>17</sup> varying thermal decomposition trend of the PPDA-PMDA (S1) aerogels with two slopes of decomposition suggest that the excess diamine content of sample, to decrease the number of repeat units to 1, was mainly consumed in altering the backbone chemistry rather than reducing the polymer chains length.
Polyimide aerogels were generally presented low thermal conductivity ranging from 30 to 50 mW $\mathrm { m ^ { - 1 } K ^ { - 1 } } .
However, unlike the other aerogels, the S2 and S7 samples presented even reduced effective thermal conductivity at higher density compared to the S1 and S6 aerogels, respectively.

As presented in Figure 11, by comparing the thermal conductivity versus density deviations, roughly similar slope of increased Keff by increased density was observed from the S2 to S3 and S4 to S5 trends on PMDA backbone as well as the S7 to S9 trend on BPDA backbone.
However, different slopes were observed from the S1 to S2 and S3 to S4 trends on PMDA backbone along with the S6 to S7 and S9 to S10 trends on BPDA backbone.

In overall, the ODA-BPDA (S10) and 50% PPDA-ODA-PMDA (S2) aerogels presented the lowest effective thermal conductivities of about 33 $( \mathrm { m } \mathrm { w } \mathrm { m } ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { K } ^ { - 1 } )$, among the studied aerogels.
The stress-strain graph of both PMDA and BPDA backbone aerogels presented in Figure 12.

As observed from Figure 12, with increasing the ODA fraction, the mechanical compression resistance and the compression absorbed energy of PMDA and BPDA backbone aerogels increased and decreased, respectively.
Due to highly brittle nature of PPDA-PMDA bonding, the samples S1 presented very short linear elasticity region.

For instance, on samples S6 with high modulus of 16.9 MPa, the plateau region of stress-strain graph was roughly eliminated, and the linear elastic region appeared to be directly continued by the densification region.

density, $\frac { \rho ^ { * } } { \rho _ { s } }$, and lower open cell content of the foams.<sup>38</sup> Increased relative density of polymeric foams was reported to increase Young's modulus, to raise the plateau stress, and to reduce the strain at which densification starts.<sup>38</sup> Furthermore, based on Gibson and Ashby classification, the polyimide aerogel stress-strain graphs were more similar to elastomeric foams rather than elastic-plastic or elastic-brittle types.<sup>38,49</sup>

Similar to the trends in Figure 12, with increasing ODA content, the compression modulus of PMDA and BPDA backbone aerogels was increased and decreased, respectively, and the compression modulus ranging from 0.18 to 16.9 MPa was observed.

Thus, the BPDA backbone polyimide aerogels with optimum backbone chemistry were able to present even higher modulus than Methyltrimethoxysilane (MTMS) reinforced silica aerogel, with maximum reported young’s modulus of 12.694 MPa.<sup>50</sup> Furthermore, both samples S3 and S9 with similar diamine content of 75% ODA and 25% PPDA, but with different dianhydride backbones presented similar compression modulus of about 4.3 MPa.

The density normalized modulus of the aerogels can be defined based on aerogel morphology as well as it’s chains properties.<sup>38</sup> Among the studied aerogels, BPDA backbone S6 and S10 aerogels presented the highest normalized modulus.
As presented in Figure 14, the normalized modulus of the PMDA backbone aerogels increased with increasing ODA fraction.

This could be due to more flexible nature of ODA-PMDA oligomers over the brittle PPDA-PMDA’s.<sup>51</sup> Furthermore, for PMDA backbone aerogels, the slope of the normalized modulus versus ODA fraction suddenly increased by increasing the ODA fraction from 75% to 87.5%.
The BPDA backbone aerogels were mainly presented higher normalized modulus than the PMDA backbone samples.
The nonlinear normalized modulus trend of hybrid BPDA backbone aerogels could be explained by varying reactivity of their diamine monomers and as a result the particulate morphology of those samples.

However, tailoring the processing parameters of the hybrid diamine BPDA backbone aerogels presented the potential to achieve enhanced network structure as well as the mechanical properties.<sup>13</sup>
Among the studied aerogels, only the PPDA-PMDA (S1) samples presented brittle assembly.
Figure 15 presents both S1 and S2 aerogels after compression test.
Therefore, no visible crack propagation was observed from the ODA-PPDA-PMDA aerogels through the compression test.
Among the aerogels the hybrid diamine BPDA backbone aerogel with 25% ODA fraction, S7, presented the highest yield stress.
However, slightly higher yield stress of S7 sample over the S6 was due to the higher density of S7 aerogels.
Furthermore, similar change of the slope between the S3 and S4 samples was observed from the yield stress versus the ODA fraction graph.

As presented in Figure 9, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) test was performed on fabricated aerogels. Due to highly crosslink nature of fabricated aerogels, the glass transition peak was barely observed in some of the samples; and specifically, for those with higher PPDA and/or PMDA content.
Furthermore, both samples S3 and S9 with similar diamine content of 75% ODA and 25% PPDA, but with different dianhydride backbones presented similar compression modulus of about 4.3 MPa.
As observed from Figure 5K to Figure 5T, the average pore size and particle diameter of the BPDA backbone aerogels were increased with increasing ODA content.<sup>13,17</sup>
The thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was performed on all studied aerogels under nitrogen environment, starting from room temperature to 750 °C at the rate of 10 °C/min.
Mechanical Compression test is performed by Instron micro-tester on aerogels samples.
With respect to ASTM D695-02a, the compression modulus of the studied aerogels was calculated from the maximum slope of stress-strain graph at region of linear elasticity, as shown in Figure 13.

Mechanical Compression test is performed by Instron micro-tester on aerogels samples. To avoid buckling, the height of each sample was modified to about 10 ± 1 mm, which was shorter than the designated height based on the ASTM standard.

Open-cell content of the aerogels is measured by helium pycnometer and calculated through Equation 2.

The fabricated aerogels presented wide range of properties with the maximum observed open cell content of 96.6% and compression modulus of 16.9 MPa along with the effective thermal conductivity and density as low as 32.5 mW/mK and 0.056 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, respectively.
In overall, the glass transition in range of $2 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$to $3 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$was observed.

Figure 16 presented the yield stress of the studied aerogels. As observed from Figure 16, the yield stress of both PMDA and BPDA backbone aerogels were roughly followed similar trends to their Young’s modulus, and the yield stress ranging from 0.03 to 1.59 MPa was observed.
